observation.garden_context: Oak Vista apiary and integrated beneficial insect habitat

identification_features: Extraordinarily long antennae — nearly body length
Large iridescent net-veined wings with intricate venation
Golden compound eyes characteristic of Chrysoperla
Wings held tent-like over body at rest

egg.description: Laid on hair-thin silk stalks standing upright from leaf surfaces
egg.color_progression: Pale green turning grey as embryo develops
egg.adaptive_significance: Stalked design prevents newly hatched larvae from eating siblings before dispersing

larva.description: Ferocious predatory larva — appearance completely unlike delicate adult
larva.remarkable_behavior: Carries debris and dead prey on back as camouflage — one of most unusual behaviors in beneficial insects

adult.attraction: Attracted to lights at night — likely explains wall observation

beneficial_classification.significance: Both adult and larval stages provide distinct ecological benefits — rare dual-stage beneficial
beneficial_classification.pest_management_value: Commercially sold for release in IPM programs — this individual arrived naturally
beneficial_classification.ipm_notes: Gardeners and farmers purchase lacewing eggs for controlled release. Natural arrival indicates high quality habitat.

habitat_requirements.nectar_sources: Shallow open flowers — umbellifers especially valuable
habitat_requirements.shelter: Dense plant structure for daytime resting
habitat_requirements.prey_availability: Aphid colonies on plants provide both larval food and adult honeydew
habitat_requirements.lighting: Attracted to artificial light at night — urban gardens with exterior lighting support adult dispersal

supporting_plants: Crimson clover (Trifolium incarnatum) — nectar and pollen
garden_connections.relationship_to_other_beneficials: Shares aphid prey resource with ladybug larvae and hoverfly larvae — complementary rather than competitive due to microhabitat differences
garden_connections.natural_enemies: Lacewing larvae themselves are preyed upon by larger predators — part of the food web

ecological_significance.indicator_value: Presence indicates diverse flowering plant community providing adult nectar resources
ecological_significance.food_web_position: Secondary predator — controls aphid populations that would otherwise explode on fruit trees and vegetables
ecological_significance.chico_context: Warm Central Valley climate supports multiple generations per season — continuous biological control through summer

census_record.breeding_confirmed: Pending — watch for stalked eggs on plant foliage
census_record.notes: Arrived naturally to habitat garden — not purchased or introduced. Confirms habitat quality sufficient to attract commercially valuable beneficial insects without intervention.
